description: What is threat modelling?
explanation: A structured look at what you are protecting, who might attack it, how, and which of those paths are worth defending first.
choice0: Structured analysis of what you protect, who might attack it, and how
choice1: Simulating an attack against production systems
choice2: Ranking employees by security awareness
choice3: Cataloguing every piece of software in use

description: Why is a defined attack surface a useful concept?
explanation: It names every point where an untrusted party can interact with the system, which is where defences and review must concentrate.
choice0: It counts how many attacks have occurred
choice1: It names every point an untrusted party can interact with, focusing defence
choice2: It measures how much data could be lost
choice3: It lists the tools an attacker would need

description: What does defence in depth mean?
explanation: Multiple independent layers of control, so the failure of any single one does not lead straight to compromise.
choice0: Investing everything in the strongest possible perimeter
choice1: Encrypting data several times over
choice2: Layering independent controls so no single failure is decisive
choice3: Keeping detailed records of every incident

description: What is the principle behind assuming breach?
explanation: Design as though an attacker is already inside, which shifts effort toward limiting movement and detecting activity rather than only keeping people out.
choice0: Design as though an attacker is already inside, and limit and detect accordingly
choice1: Notify customers before any breach is confirmed
choice2: Treat every employee as a suspect
choice3: Replace prevention entirely with insurance

description: What is the central idea of zero trust?
explanation: Nothing is trusted purely because of where it sits on the network; every request is authenticated and authorised on its own merits.
choice0: No employee is given any access without approval
choice1: Network location grants no trust; every request is verified on its own merits
choice2: All external traffic is blocked by default
choice3: Passwords are replaced entirely by biometrics

description: Why is the traditional trusted internal network model considered inadequate now?
explanation: Once the perimeter is crossed, a flat trusted interior lets an intruder move freely, and remote work and cloud have dissolved the perimeter anyway.
choice0: A crossed perimeter leaves a freely traversable interior, and the perimeter has dissolved
choice1: Internal networks are slower than cloud services
choice2: Firewalls are no longer manufactured
choice3: Internal traffic cannot be encrypted

description: What is lateral movement?
explanation: After gaining an initial foothold, an attacker moves from system to system toward more valuable targets.
choice0: Copying data between two directories
choice1: Moving a service between data centres
choice2: Moving from an initial foothold toward more valuable systems
choice3: Rotating credentials across an organisation

description: Why does reusing the same local administrator password across machines aid lateral movement?
explanation: One compromised machine hands the attacker credentials that work everywhere else with the same password.
choice0: Compromising one machine yields credentials that work on all the others
choice1: It makes the password easier to guess
choice2: It prevents logging from working
choice3: It disables the local firewall

description: What is privilege escalation?
explanation: Gaining rights beyond those originally held, moving from a limited account toward administrative control.
choice0: Requesting extra access through a formal process
choice1: Gaining rights beyond those originally held
choice2: Being promoted to an administrative role
choice3: Increasing the priority of a running process

description: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
explanation: A flaw being exploited before the vendor has released a fix, so patching is not yet an available defence.
choice0: A flaw discovered on the day software is released
choice1: A flaw that is fixed within one day
choice2: A flaw that affects only one customer
choice3: A flaw exploited before any fix exists

description: What is the value of a CVSS score, and its main limitation?
explanation: It gives a comparable severity rating, but it says nothing about whether that flaw matters in your specific environment.
choice0: It gives comparable severity, but ignores whether the flaw matters in your context
choice1: It measures how long a fix will take
choice2: It counts how many systems are affected
choice3: It states whether an exploit exists

description: Why should patching be prioritised by exploitability and exposure rather than severity alone?
explanation: A medium-severity flaw on an internet-facing system with a public exploit is more urgent than a critical one on an isolated machine.
choice0: Because severity scores are usually wrong
choice1: Because a lower-severity flaw that is exposed and exploitable can be the greater real risk
choice2: Because critical patches take longer to install
choice3: Because exposure cannot be measured

description: What is responsible disclosure?
explanation: A researcher reports a flaw privately and allows time for a fix before publishing details.
choice0: Publishing a flaw immediately so users can react
choice1: Reporting a flaw only to a regulator
choice2: Reporting privately and allowing time for a fix before publishing
choice3: Selling the flaw to the highest bidder

description: What distinguishes a penetration test from a vulnerability scan?
explanation: A scan enumerates known weaknesses automatically; a penetration test has skilled people chain weaknesses together to reach a real objective.
choice0: A scan lists known weaknesses; a test chains them to reach a real objective
choice1: A scan is manual and a test is automated
choice2: A scan is performed by attackers, a test by defenders
choice3: They are the same thing under different names

description: Why must a penetration test be formally authorised in writing before it begins?
explanation: The same activity is a criminal offence without authorisation; the scope and permission define the boundary.
choice0: To arrange payment in advance
choice1: Because the same activity without authorisation is a criminal offence
choice2: Because testers need physical building access
choice3: To decide which tools may be purchased

description: What does a red team exercise measure that a penetration test usually does not?
explanation: It tests whether the defenders actually detect and respond, not just whether a weakness exists.
choice0: How many vulnerabilities exist in total
choice1: Whether software is correctly licensed
choice2: Whether the defenders detect and respond to a realistic attack
choice3: How quickly patches can be deployed

description: What problem does asymmetric cryptography solve that symmetric does not?
explanation: Two parties can communicate securely without having agreed a shared secret beforehand.
choice0: Establishing security without a shared secret agreed in advance
choice1: Encrypting large volumes of data quickly
choice2: Storing keys on disk safely
choice3: Compressing data before transmission

description: Why do real systems typically combine asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
explanation: Asymmetric methods exchange a key safely, then fast symmetric encryption protects the bulk of the traffic.
choice0: Because one of them is always broken
choice1: Asymmetric exchanges the key safely, symmetric then encrypts the bulk efficiently
choice2: Because regulators require both
choice3: Because symmetric keys cannot be generated alone

description: What does a certificate authority actually vouch for?
explanation: That a particular public key belongs to the named domain, which is what stops an impostor presenting their own key.
choice0: That the websites content is accurate
choice1: That the site owner is a reputable business
choice2: That a public key genuinely belongs to the named domain
choice3: That the site is free of malware

description: What is certificate pinning intended to prevent?
explanation: It refuses connections signed by any certificate other than the expected one, blocking interception even by a trusted-but-compromised authority.
choice0: Interception using a certificate from a compromised or coerced authority
choice1: Certificates expiring unexpectedly
choice2: Users ignoring browser warnings
choice3: Traffic being compressed in transit

description: Why is rolling your own encryption algorithm strongly discouraged?
explanation: Cryptography fails silently: a scheme can look fine and be trivially broken, and only sustained public scrutiny establishes otherwise.
choice0: Because it takes too long to write
choice1: Because flaws are invisible without sustained public scrutiny
choice2: Because custom algorithms run slowly
choice3: Because it requires specialist hardware

description: What does forward secrecy protect against?
explanation: If a long-term key is later compromised, past recorded sessions still cannot be decrypted.
choice0: Attackers predicting future keys
choice1: Certificates being issued to the wrong domain
choice2: Passwords being reused across sites
choice3: Past recorded traffic being decrypted after a key is later stolen

description: Why is input validation on the client insufficient on its own?
explanation: Anyone can bypass the client entirely and send requests directly, so the server must validate everything again.
choice0: Requests can be sent directly, bypassing the client entirely
choice1: Client validation is slower
choice2: Browsers disable validation by default
choice3: It only works for text fields

description: What is insecure direct object reference?
explanation: The application exposes an identifier and does not check that the requester is entitled to that record, so changing the number reveals someone elses data.
choice0: Referring to an object before it has been created
choice1: Exposing an identifier without checking the requester is entitled to that record
choice2: Storing objects without encryption
choice3: Linking to an external website directly

description: Why should error messages shown to users avoid technical detail?
explanation: Stack traces and database errors hand an attacker a map of the internals, while telling the user nothing useful.
choice0: Because they are hard to translate
choice1: Because they slow the application down
choice2: Because they reveal internal details that help an attacker
choice3: Because users cannot read them

description: What is the security argument for rate limiting a login endpoint?
explanation: It makes automated guessing and credential stuffing impractical by capping how many attempts can be made.
choice0: It makes automated password guessing and credential stuffing impractical
choice1: It reduces the servers electricity use
choice2: It prevents users forgetting their passwords
choice3: It removes the need for multi-factor authentication

description: Why should a failed login say the credentials were wrong, without saying which part?
explanation: Distinguishing them confirms which accounts exist, which is useful reconnaissance for an attacker.
choice0: To keep the message short
choice1: Because saying which part was wrong confirms whether an account exists
choice2: Because the system cannot tell which was wrong
choice3: To comply with password length rules

description: What is the risk of storing secrets in application source code?
explanation: Anyone with repository access, including its full history, gets the secret, and it usually spreads to backups and forks.
choice0: The code becomes harder to compile
choice1: Secrets in code cannot be encrypted
choice2: The application starts more slowly
choice3: Anyone with repository access, including history, obtains the secret

description: What does a SIEM system do?
explanation: It centralises logs from many systems and correlates them, so patterns invisible in any single log become detectable.
choice0: Centralises and correlates logs so cross-system patterns become visible
choice1: Blocks malicious traffic at the network edge
choice2: Encrypts data at rest across the estate
choice3: Manages user passwords centrally

description: Why is a very high false positive rate dangerous in a detection system?
explanation: Analysts become desensitised and start dismissing alerts, so the real one is missed among the noise.
choice0: It consumes too much storage
choice1: Analysts become desensitised and dismiss the real alert among the noise
choice2: It slows the network down
choice3: It prevents logs from being written

description: What is the difference between signature-based and behaviour-based detection?
explanation: Signatures match known-bad patterns and miss novel attacks; behavioural detection flags departures from normal and catches unknowns at the cost of more false alarms.
choice0: Signature detection is manual, behavioural is automatic
choice1: Signature detection works on networks, behavioural on endpoints
choice2: Signatures match known patterns; behaviour flags departures from normal
choice3: They differ only in how results are displayed

description: Why does dwell time matter as a security metric?
explanation: The longer an intruder goes undetected, the more access they accumulate and the greater the eventual damage.
choice0: Longer undetected presence means more accumulated access and greater damage
choice1: It measures how long patching takes
choice2: It measures how long staff spend on training
choice3: It determines the cost of insurance

description: Why is an unused but still-enabled service account a notable risk?
explanation: Nobody watches it, its credentials rarely rotate, and it often holds broad permissions, making it an ideal quiet foothold.
choice0: It consumes a software licence
choice1: Nobody watches it, its credentials rarely rotate, and it often has broad rights
choice2: It slows down authentication for everyone
choice3: It cannot be removed once created

description: What is the security benefit of short-lived credentials?
explanation: A stolen credential is only useful for a short window, which sharply limits the value of theft.
choice0: A stolen credential is only useful briefly
choice1: They are easier for users to remember
choice2: They remove the need for access reviews
choice3: They can be shared safely between people

description: Why is just-in-time privileged access preferred over standing administrative rights?
explanation: Elevated rights exist only for the moment they are needed and are logged, so a compromised account is usually not an administrator.
choice0: It reduces the number of administrators required
choice1: It removes the need for multi-factor authentication
choice2: Rights exist only when needed and are logged, so a compromised account is usually unprivileged
choice3: It speeds up administrative tasks

description: Why are insider risks difficult to address with perimeter controls?
explanation: The activity comes from someone already authorised, so it looks legitimate to controls designed to keep outsiders out.
choice0: The activity comes from an authorised person and looks legitimate
choice1: Insiders always work outside business hours
choice2: Perimeter controls cannot log internal traffic
choice3: Insiders never use company accounts

description: What distinguishes a malicious insider from a negligent one, and why does it matter?
explanation: One intends harm and will try to hide it; the other makes mistakes. Detection and prevention differ accordingly.
choice0: Only the malicious one causes real damage
choice1: One intends harm and conceals it, the other errs, so the responses differ
choice2: Negligent insiders are always junior staff
choice3: There is no practical difference

description: What do RTO and RPO specify in a recovery plan?
explanation: RTO is how quickly service must be restored; RPO is how much recent data you can afford to lose.
choice0: The number of backups and their retention period
choice1: The cost and duration of an outage
choice2: How fast service must be restored, and how much recent data may be lost
choice3: How often the plan must be reviewed and by whom

description: Why must backups be isolated from the systems they protect?
explanation: Ransomware deliberately seeks out and encrypts reachable backups, so a connected backup can be destroyed along with everything else.
choice0: Ransomware targets reachable backups, destroying them with everything else
choice1: Isolated backups restore more quickly
choice2: It reduces the storage required
choice3: Regulators forbid backups on the same site

description: What does an immutable backup guarantee?
explanation: Once written it cannot be altered or deleted for a set period, even by an administrator account.
choice0: It is stored in more than one country
choice1: It cannot be altered or deleted for a set period, even by an administrator
choice2: It is compressed to save space
choice3: It is encrypted with a rotating key

description: Why is preserving evidence a priority early in an incident?
explanation: Rebuilding or rebooting destroys the traces needed to establish what happened and how far it went.
choice0: Because regulators require a full disk image
choice1: Because evidence can be sold to researchers
choice2: Because it speeds up recovery
choice3: Because rebuilding destroys the traces needed to understand the scope

description: Why should incident communication use a channel separate from the affected systems?
explanation: If the attacker is inside the normal systems, they can read the response plan as it is written.
choice0: An intruder inside the normal systems could read the response as it unfolds
choice1: The normal channel is usually too slow
choice2: It reduces the load on the mail server
choice3: Regulators require a separate channel

description: Why is disclosing a breach to affected people promptly usually the right call?
explanation: They can protect themselves, and concealment compounds both the harm and the legal and reputational consequences.
choice0: Because disclosure ends the incident
choice1: They can protect themselves, and concealment worsens the harm and the consequences
choice2: Because it transfers liability to them
choice3: Because it prevents the attacker returning

description: What does a software bill of materials give a defender?
explanation: A list of every component in a product, so when a flaw is announced you can tell in minutes whether you are affected.
choice0: A list of the licences a product requires
choice1: A budget for the software estate
choice2: A component inventory, so exposure to a new flaw can be assessed quickly
choice3: A record of who wrote each module

description: Why is a compromised build pipeline especially serious?
explanation: Malicious code is signed and distributed through the legitimate channel, so it inherits the trust everyone places in the vendor.
choice0: The malicious code is signed and shipped through the trusted channel
choice1: Build servers hold customer data
choice2: Pipelines cannot be monitored
choice3: It prevents future releases entirely

description: What is typosquatting in a package repository?
explanation: An attacker publishes a package with a name close to a popular one, so a typo installs their code instead.
choice0: Publishing a package with no source code
choice1: Publishing a package named close to a popular one, so a typo installs it
choice2: Copying a package under a new licence
choice3: Uploading the same package many times

description: Why is a formal risk acceptance decision better than an unaddressed known risk?
explanation: It puts the decision with someone accountable, on the record, with a date to revisit, rather than leaving it to drift unowned.
choice0: It places the decision with someone accountable, on record and revisited
choice1: It removes the risk entirely
choice2: It transfers the risk to the vendor
choice3: It satisfies every regulatory requirement

description: Why does compliance with a standard not equal being secure?
explanation: A standard sets a minimum baseline at a point in time; attackers do not confine themselves to what the checklist covers.
choice0: Because standards are usually written incorrectly
choice1: A standard is a point-in-time minimum, and attackers ignore its boundaries
choice2: Because compliance is voluntary
choice3: Because auditors do not test technical controls

description: What is the security argument for making the secure path the easy path?
explanation: Controls that obstruct real work get circumvented, so usability determines whether a control is actually effective.
choice0: Easy controls are cheaper to buy
choice1: It reduces the number of staff needed
choice2: Controls that obstruct work get bypassed, so usability decides effectiveness
choice3: It removes the need for training

description: Why is an asset inventory considered a foundational control?
explanation: You cannot patch, monitor or protect what you do not know exists, so unknown systems become the weak point.
choice0: You cannot patch, monitor or protect systems you do not know exist
choice1: It is required before purchasing insurance
choice2: It reduces software licence costs
choice3: It replaces the need for vulnerability scanning
